title: Joshua J. Taylor
text:
I am a research associate at the Oden Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences at the University of Texas at Austin. I am also affiliated with CosmicAI, the NSF–Simons AI Institute for Cosmic Origins, and with the Oden Institute’s Center for Scientific Machine Learning.
My research is in unsupervised learning of scientific data that are large, high-dimensional, and noisy, where no labels exist to guide scientific analysis. I am drawn to this problem because unsupervised learning is the most direct route to discovery. It can surface populations and physical regimes that no one thought to look for, but also brings its own assumptions about what counts as structure. My own methods, built on prototype learning, learned connectivity graphs, and low-dimensional embeddings, are designed to be rooted in as much data evidence as possible.
I work primarily inside astronomy, specifically parsing the spectral cubes, infrared surveys, and simulations of star-formation astrophysics to learn how gas in molecular clouds assembles into stars. My long-term goal is a general paradigm for physics-informed unsupervised learning.

title: Research
text: Modern scientific instruments and simulations produce data that are large, high-dimensional, and noisy. Much of what a scientist wants from such data depends on knowing what they contain, namely which populations or physical regimes are present and what those imply about physics. When no labels exist, that question falls to unsupervised learning, which in turn hands an analyst every degree of freedom a label would otherwise have fixed, such as data resolutions, neighborhood sizes, cluster counts, and model forms. My work builds methods that let the data make those choices.

title: Research
text:
The Methods
My methods begin by compressing a large, noisy data set into a small number of representative observations that remain in the units of the data. Pooling observations this way suppresses noise and leaves a representation a scientist can inspect directly, rather than a latent space that has to be decoded. From these representatives the methods learn how the data are organized, which parts of the data space connect to which, and that learned organization is what drives everything downstream, from visualization to clustering.
Three goals run through this work. The first is to make the consequential choices in an unsupervised analysis, such as how finely to resolve the data, how large a neighborhood counts as local, and how many groups are present, into quantities the data determine through explicit statistical criteria rather than settings an analyst tunes. The second is to keep the results in a form a scientist can interpret directly, so that a representative observation can be measured like data and a cluster can be checked against what is known about the system that produced it. The third is to attach evidence to what the methods find, both by separating genuine structure from structured noise and by quantifying the uncertainty of the results, so that a discovery made without labels can still be defended.

title: Research
text:
The Science
My scientific work studies the star formation process, where the main question is how the diffuse gas in a galaxy turns into stars. That process runs from clouds of gas hundreds of light-years across down to the dense cores, a fraction of a light-year wide, in which individual stars are born. The data that trace it come from radio and infrared telescopes and from simulations that follow the gas through time. Each step along that path, from cloud to core to star, raises questions that unsupervised methods are suited to answer, because the categories of interest (the regimes of the gas and the phases of a core’s life) are not known in advance.
Three of those questions have organized my work. How is the dense gas within a cloud structured and fed, and what do the motions of its different molecular species say about material flowing in to form stars? What happens to a dense core over its lifetime? Some cores go on to form stars, but some disperse back into molecular gas. Can this fate be anticipated from a core’s present state? And once stars have formed, how can we study them (observationally) when most of them are faint and incompletely observed? The methods described above have let my collaborators and me answer each of these with less reliance on hand-tuned analysis than the field is used to, and in several cases with results that standard astronomical analyses miss.

title: Research
text:
Where this is going
Physics-informed supervised learning now has a settled vocabulary for where physics enters a model. Its unsupervised counterpart does not exist yet, and building it is my long-term research program. The result would be methods in which physical constraints shape how structure is discovered without foreclosing the discoveries that only unsupervised learning can make. That requires a statistical accounting of how much of a result the physics decided and how much the data did, and that accounting is what I am starting on now.

title: Software
text:
Open-source Python packages behind the methods, each with documentation and tutorials.
soumap · GitHub
Self-Organizing UMAP: a hybrid SOM/UMAP algorithm that jointly learns data prototypes and their low-dimensional embedding, with multiview clustering (MPEC).
vqlp · GitHub
Vector quantization under arbitrary Lp metrics, with recall quantities: prototype assignments, quantization error, receptive fields, and the connectivity graph.
gtsom · GitHub
General-topology Self-Organizing Maps: SOM training on arbitrary output-space geometries.
